name: Masjid Al-Dahab
summary:
Masjid Al-Dahab (Arabic: مسجد الذهب, Mosque of Gold) — an informal name for the Al-Azhar Mosque annex or a specific prayer hall in Cairo, Egypt, or alternatively a mosque in Morocco known as the 'Golden Mosque' — represents the tradition of naming mosques with evocative Arabic phrases that capture architectural features, spiritual qualities, or historical associations. The 'Dahab' (gold) name in mosque context typically refers to gilded decoration, golden dome or minarets, or a location with historical associations to golden age prosperity.

Mosques named with 'Dahab' or golden associations reflect the Islamic architectural tradition of using precious metal ornamentation to express the mosque's status as the house of God deserving the most beautiful physical expression. The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem (completed 691 CE), with its golden dome covered in gold-anodized aluminum (original gilded tiles), is the most famous example of 'golden' Islamic architecture conveying divine presence through precious material.

In Egypt, Cairo has historically been associated with gold through the medieval Islamic trade economy — Cairo's markets (khans) were the commercial hub of the medieval Islamic world, and its mosques reflected the wealth generated by trade. Any mosque bearing the 'Dahab' name in Cairo participates in this tradition of associating the mosque with the highest material and spiritual values of Islamic civilization.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Masjid Al-Dahab — representing the Islamic architectural tradition of associating mosques with gold and precious beauty as expressions of divine presence — is locally significant as a monument to the Islamic sacred architecture's use of material beauty for spiritual aspiration.
